A Jordan normal form of a complex n×n matrix A is a similarity transformation P−1AP=J in which J is a direct sum of Jordan blocks
Jr​(λ)=​λ0​1λ​⋱⋱​01λ​​.
(1)
For each eigenvalue, the multiset of block sizes is uniquely determined by A; only the order of the blocks is arbitrary. The change-of-basis matrix P is generally not unique.
For the given matrix, expansion of the characteristic polynomial gives
det(tI−A)=(t−1)2(t−2),A−I=​−8717​3−2−6​−5511​​.
(2)
The upper-left 2×2 minor of A−I is −5, so its rank is 2 and the eigenspace for 1 has dimension 1. Thus the two occurrences of the eigenvalue 1 belong to a single size-2 Jordan block. More explicitly, the Jordan chain and the remaining eigenvector can be chosen as
v1​=(1,1,−1)T,v2​=(1,3,0)T,v3​=(0,5,3)T,(A−I)v1​=0,(A−I)v2​=v1​,Av3​=2v3​.
(3)
Consequently, with P=(v1​ v2​ v3​), for which detP=1, the answer is

2G OurBigBook.com
Write qn​(X)=1+X+⋯+Xn−1, a monic primitive polynomial. If n=ab with a,b>1, grouping terms gives a factorization in the polynomial ring Z[X]:
qn​(X)=(1+X+⋯+Xa−1)(1+Xa+⋯+X(b−1)a).
(5)
Both factors have positive degree, so qn​ is not an irreducible polynomial.
Conversely, if n=p is a prime number, change variables by X=Y+1. The binomial theorem gives
qp​(Y+1)=Y(Y+1)p−1​=p+(2p​)Y+⋯+(p−1p​)Yp−2+Yp−1.
(6)
Every coefficient except the leading one is divisible by p, because p∣(kp​) for 1≤k<p, whereas the constant coefficient p is not divisible by p2. The Eisenstein criterion makes this polynomial irreducible over Q. The substitution X↦Y+1 is an invertible ring homomorphism, so qp​ is also irreducible over Q; the Gauss lemma for polynomials transfers this to Z[X]. Hence
qn​ is irreducible over Z⟺n is prime.​
(7)

Words: 153
3F OurBigBook.com
Both functionals are finite on X: a continuous function on the compact metric space [0,1] is bounded and integrable. Homogeneity follows from ∣af∣=∣a∣∣f∣, and the triangle inequality follows by integrating, or taking the supremum of, ∣f+g∣≤∣f∣+∣g∣. Each is nonnegative. If ∥f∥∞​=0, then f vanishes everywhere. If a continuous function f is nonzero at some point, continuity supplies an interval of positive length on which ∣f∣ is bounded below by a positive number; hence ∥f∥1​>0. Thus both are norms.
For the nonnegative fn​, direct integration gives the L1 norm
∥fn​∥1​=n∫01​(tn−tn+1)dt=(n+1)(n+2)n​⟶0.
(8)
Therefore fn​⟶0 in ∥⋅∥1​​. On the other hand, differentiation places the maximum of tn(1−t) at t=n/(n+1), giving the supremum norm
∥fn​∥∞​=(n+1n​)n+1⟶e−1.
(9)
For t<1, exponential decay implies ntn(1−t)→0, while fn​(1)=0. Thus the pointwise convergence is to zero throughout [0,1]. Any convergence in the supremum norm would imply uniform convergence, hence the same pointwise limit zero, contradicting the displayed positive limiting norm. Therefore there is no convergence in the supremum norm.

4E (Complex Analysis)

Words: 191 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 191
4E OurBigBook.com
Set h=f−g, an entire function. By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, a subsequence of the distinct zeros zi​ converges to a point a in the closed unit disc. An analytic function has a convergent Taylor series in a neighbourhood of each point. If the first nonzero coefficient of h at a had index m, then
h(z)=(z−a)mk(z),k(a)=0,
(10)
with k analytic and nonzero in a sufficiently small disc. The zero a would then be isolated, contradicting the accumulating distinct zeros. All Taylor coefficients at a vanish, so h vanishes on a disc.
To justify continuation across the whole plane, let Z be the set of points at which h vanishes on a neighbourhood. This set is nonempty and open. It is also closed: if points of Z tend to b, continuity of each derivative gives h(m)(b)=0 for every m, and the Taylor series at b gives a zero neighbourhood. Since C is a connected space, Z=C. This proves the identity theorem here and gives f≡g​.
Without boundedness, the distinct zeros need not have an accumulation point in the plane. For example,
f(z)=sin(πz),g(z)=0,zi​=i (i=1,2,…)​
(11)
are distinct entire functions agreeing at all the indicated positive integers.

6A (Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 138
6A OurBigBook.com
For a time-independent Quantum Hamiltonian, a stationary state is an energy eigenstate. The Schrödinger equation separates its time dependence as
ψ(x,t)=e−iEt/ℏχ(x),Hχ=Eχ.
(16)
Its probability density ∣ψ(x,t)∣2=∣χ(x)∣2 is time independent. Linearity of the Schrödinger equation gives
ψ(x,t)=2​1​(e−iE1​t/ℏχ1​(x)+e−iE2​t/ℏχ2​(x)).​
(17)
Put Ajk​=∫−∞∞​χj∗​Aχk​dx. The operator for a time-independent observable is a Hermitian operator, so A21​=A12​​. Substituting the evolved wavefunction into the expectation value gives
⟨ψ,Aψ⟩=21​(A11​+A22​+ei(E1​−E2​)t/ℏA12​+e−i(E1​−E2​)t/ℏA12​​),
(18)
and therefore, for a normalized state,
⟨A⟩ψ​=2A11​+A22​​+Re(ei(E1​−E2​)t/ℏA12​).​
(19)
The normalization is automatic for orthogonal χ1​,χ2​, in particular when E1​=E2​: self-adjointness of H gives (E1​−E2​)⟨χ1​,χ2​⟩=0. If the energies coincide, normalization of the individual eigenstates alone does not ensure normalization of their displayed sum; its squared norm is 1+Re⟨χ1​,χ2​⟩. For a nonzero sum not having unit norm, the physical expectation value is the displayed numerator divided by this squared norm. With orthonormal energy states, the stated formula holds in both the distinct and degenerate cases.

The differential Gauss law is ∇⋅E=ρ/ϵ0​. On a large ball BR​, the product rule and ∇ϕ=−E give
ρϕ=ϵ0​∇⋅(ϕE)+ϵ0​∣E∣2.
(20)
The divergence theorem consequently expresses the electrostatic energy as
21​∫BR​​ρϕdV=2ϵ0​​∫BR​​∣E∣2dV+2ϵ0​​∫∂BR​​ϕE⋅ndS.
(21)
For a localized charge distribution with the electric potential chosen to vanish at infinity, ϕ=O(R−1) and E=O(R−2), so the surface term is O(R−1) and tends to zero. More generally, it suffices to assume that this boundary integral vanishes. Passing to all space gives
U=2ϵ0​​∫R3​∣E∣2dV.​
(22)
The physical decay and potential reference are relevant: E→0 by itself does not specify the additive constant in ϕ. Adding a constant C changes the charge-based expression by CQ/2 when the total charge is Q, while leaving the field unchanged. The zero-at-infinity potential is the usual reference implicit in this all-space electrostatic energy formula.

With x=cosθ, the weighted inner product for the Chebyshev polynomials becomes
∫−11​1−x2​Tn​(x)Tm​(x)​dx=∫0π​cos(nθ)cos(mθ)dθ.
(25)
The identity 2cos(nθ)cos(mθ)=cos((n−m)θ)+cos((n+m)θ) and the vanishing of ∫0π​cos(kθ)dθ for positive integers k give zero when n=m, π/2 when n=m>0, and π when n=m=0. Thus
∫−11​1−x2​Tn​Tm​​dx=2π​δnm​(1+δn0​).​
(26)
For Gaussian quadrature, choose the n distinct nodes as the zeros of the degree-n orthogonal polynomial for the weight, here Tn​, and choose the weights as the weighted integrals of their Lagrange interpolation basis functions. If a polynomial p has degree at most 2n−1, divide it as p=qTn​+r, where both q and r have degree at most n−1. Orthogonality makes the integral of qTn​ zero, while its quadrature sum also vanishes; interpolation integrates r exactly. This proves degree 2n−1 exactness. It is optimal because the squared nodal polynomial, of degree 2n, has zero quadrature sum and strictly positive integral.
For n=3, T3​(x)=4x3−3x, so the nodes are −3​/2,0,3​/2. Their interpolation basis functions are
ℓ−​(x)=32​x(x−23​​),ℓ0​(x)=1−34​x2,ℓ+​(x)=32​x(x+23​​).
(27)
The weighted zeroth and second moments are π and π/2, and the first moment is zero. Integrating these three basis functions gives equal weights π/3, hence the Chebyshev–Gauss quadrature rule
∫−11​1−x2​f(x)​dx≈3π​[f(−23​​)+f(0)+f(23​​)],​

which is exact for every polynomial of degree at most 5.

9H (Markov Chains)

9H OurBigBook.com
The communicating classes are T={1,2}, B={3,4} and C={5,6,7}. The class T is open: it can reach B or C and cannot be reached from either. To remain in T for two steps has probability 1/6, so Pi​(X2k​∈T)=(1/6)k for i∈T. Its states are transient states. All returns within T have even length and a two-step return is possible, so their period of a state in a Markov chain is 2.
The closed communicating class B alternates deterministically between 3 and 4, and therefore consists of positive recurrent states of period 2. The class C is finite, closed and irreducible, so its states are also positive recurrent states. The self-loop at 7 gives period 1 there, and the period is constant on a communicating class, so every state of C has period 1.
For C, solve the stationary distribution equations:
π5​=21​π7​,π6​=π5​,π7​=π6​+21​π7​,π5​+π6​+π7​=1.
(29)
Hence (π5​,π6​,π7​)=(1/4,1/4,1/2). Finite irreducibility and aperiodicity imply convergence to this stationary distribution from any state of C. If hi​ is the probability of eventually entering C, the Markov property gives
h1​=21​h2​+41​,h2​=31​h1​+61​,
(30)
so h1​=2/5 and h2​=3/10. Conditioning on the finite entrance time and then letting the remaining time tend to infinity proves that the limiting probabilities in C are hi​πj​. The probability of entrance after a large cutoff tends to zero, which justifies this conditioning limit.
For B, convergence depends on the parity balance on entry to a period-two Markov class. Entry always occurs at 3. Starting from 1, the probabilities of first entry at time 2k+1 and at time 2k+2 are both 41​(1/6)k. Each parity therefore has total probability 3/10, so both p13(n)​ and p14(n)​ tend to 3/10, despite the recurrent class being periodic. Starting from 2, the corresponding odd- and even-entry probabilities are 21​(1/6)k and 121​(1/6)k, with totals 3/5 and 1/10. Consequently
(p23(2k)​,p24(2k)​)⟶(1/10,3/5),(p23(2k+1)​,p24(2k+1)​)⟶(3/5,1/10),
(31)
so neither limit exists. From 3 or 4, the probabilities at 3 and 4 alternate between zero and one; from C they are identically zero. Finally every probability of being in T tends to zero, from all starting states.
All 49 requested conclusions are encoded below, with ∗ denoting a nonexistent limit:
(n→∞lim​pij(n)​)i,j=17​=​0000000​0000000​3/10∗∗∗000​3/10∗∗∗000​1/103/40001/41/41/4​1/103/40001/41/41/4​1/53/20001/21/21/2​​.​
(32)
The class classification is T: transient, period 2; B: recurrent, period 2; C: recurrent, period 1.

10E OurBigBook.com
A Hermitian matrix satisfies A=A†, where † means conjugate transpose. If Av=λv with v=0, then v†Av=λ∥v∥2 is real, since it equals its complex conjugate v†A†v. Thus every eigenvalue is real. To prove the finite-dimensional spectral theorem, choose a unit eigenvector v; one exists because the complex characteristic polynomial has a root. Its orthogonal complement is invariant, since for w⊥v,
v†Aw=(Av)†w=λv†w=0.
(33)
The restriction to that complement is again Hermitian. Induction on dimension supplies an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A=Udiag(λ1​,…,λn​)U† for a unitary matrix U.
In this basis, x†Ax=∑i​λi​∣(U†x)i​∣2. Therefore A>0⟺λi​>0 for every i​. In that case the square root of a matrix
C=Udiag(λ1​​,…,λn​​)U†
(34)
is Hermitian, positive definite and satisfies C2=A. For uniqueness, any positive-definite Hermitian D satisfying D2=A commutes with A and hence preserves each eigenspace of A. Its restriction to the λ-eigenspace is Hermitian, and its positive eigenvalues all solve μ2=λ. Thus that restriction is λ​I, forcing D=C. This is the principal square root of a positive semidefinite matrix, here strictly positive definite.
Now let D=B​ and X=C−D. Expanding without assuming that C and D commute gives
CX+XC=2C2−CD−DC=(A−B)+X2.
(35)
The Hermitian matrix X has X2≥0 because v†X2v=∥Xv∥2, whereas A−B>0. Hence CX+XC>0. If Xv=μv, v=0, then
0<v†(CX+XC)v=2μv†Cv.
(36)
Since C>0, every real eigenvalue μ of X is positive. The positive-eigenvalue criterion now gives the strict finite-dimensional operator monotonicity of the square root:
CX+XC>0,A​−B​=X>0.​
(37)

11G OurBigBook.com
An R-module M is a free module if it has a basis (ei​)i∈I​: every m∈M has a unique expression as a finite sum ∑i​ri​ei​, with ri​∈R. Equivalently, it is a direct sum of copies of R. Let q:M→M/N be the quotient map. When M/N is free, choose a basis (f​j​) and lifts fj​∈M. The universal property of a free module defines an R-linear map s:M/N→M by s(∑j​rj​f​j​)=∑j​rj​fj​. It satisfies q∘s=id, so every m∈M decomposes uniquely as
m=(m−s(q(m)))+s(q(m)),m−s(q(m))∈N.
(38)
This gives a split short exact sequence and M≅N⊕(M/N). If N is also free, the union of its basis and the lifted quotient basis is a basis of M: spanning follows from the decomposition, and applying q to a putative relation kills all quotient coefficients before independence in N kills the remaining ones. Thus free submodule and free quotient imply a free module.
For the first claim, take R=Z and
M=Z,N=2Z,M′=Z⊕Z/2Z,N′=Z⊕{0}.
(39)
Here N≅N′≅Z are free modules and M/N≅M′/N′≅Z/2Z. But M is a torsion-free module, whereas M′ contains the nonzero torsion element (0,1). Therefore claim (1) is false.
For the second claim, the same lifting construction works without assuming that N is free. Since both isomorphic quotient modules are free, it yields
M≅N⊕(M/N)≅N′⊕(M′/N′)≅M′.
(40)
Thus claim (2) is true. Equivalently, this uses the fact that free modules are projective.

δE=∫ab​[(2Eu​u˙2+2Fu​u˙v˙+Gu​v˙2​−dtd​(Eu˙+Fv˙))η+(2Ev​u˙2+2Fv​u˙v˙+Gv​v˙2​−dtd​(Fu˙+Gv˙))ξ]dt.

dtd​(Eu˙+Fv˙)=21​(Eu​u˙2+2Fu​u˙v˙+Gu​v˙2),dtd​(Fu˙+Gv˙)=21​(Ev​u˙2+2Fv​u˙v˙+Gv​v˙2).​

The angle θ between the oriented coordinate tangent vectors satisfies cosθ=F/EG​. The constant-angle assumption therefore gives F=kE​G​ for a constant k. The first fundamental form is positive definite, so EG−F2>0 and hence ∣k∣<1. Substitution into the geodesic coordinate grid identities from part (i) gives
k(E​)v​=(G​)u​,k(G​)u​=(E​)v​.

Ev​=0=Gu​.​

Two norms ∥⋅∥a​,∥⋅∥b​ are Lipschitz equivalent norms when constants c,C>0 satisfy c∥x∥a​≤∥x∥b​≤C∥x∥a​ for every vector x. Applying these inequalities to xj​−xk​ shows that a sequence is a Cauchy sequence for one norm exactly when it is so for the other; applying them to xj​−x likewise equates convergence. If one norm is complete, a Cauchy sequence for the other converges using the first norm and hence also the second. Interchanging the norms proves completeness is preserved in both directions.
Write x=∑i​xi​ei​ and set C=∑i​∥ei​∥. If ∥x∥2​=1, then ∣xi​∣≤1, and the triangle inequality gives
∥x∥≤∑i​∣xi​∣∥ei​∥≤C.
(48)
Scaling a nonzero x gives ∥x∥≤C∥x∥2​ for every x. The reverse triangle inequality now implies
​∥x∥−∥y∥​≤∥x−y∥≤C∥x−y∥2​,
(49)
so x↦∥x∥ is continuous, indeed Lipschitz, in the Euclidean norm.
Suppose there were no positive lower bound on the Euclidean unit sphere. We could choose xj​ with ∥xj​∥2​=1 but ∥xj​∥<1/j. The Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem supplies a subsequence converging in the Euclidean norm to x. Continuity of both norms gives ∥x∥2​=1 and ∥x∥=0, contradicting definiteness. m∥x∥2​≤∥x∥≤(i=1∑n​∥ei​∥)∥x∥2​for every x∈Rn.​

14F (Metric and Topological Spaces)

14F OurBigBook.com
A basis of a topology is a family B of open sets such that every open set is a union of members of B. Equivalently, whenever x∈U and U is open, there is B∈B with x∈B⊆U. For a metric space, all open balls form a basis. For the product topology on X×Y, the rectangles U×V with U,V open in their respective factors form a basis; rectangles made from factor bases also suffice.
If C⊆X and D⊆Y are countable dense subsets, then C×D is countable. Every nonempty basic rectangle meets it, since U∩C and V∩D are nonempty. Every nonempty open set contains such a rectangle, proving that a product of two separable spaces is separable.
Suppose a metric space has a countable dense set C. The balls B(c,r) with c∈C and positive rational r form a countable basis. Indeed, given x∈U open, choose ϵ>0 with B(x,ϵ)⊆U, then choose c∈C with d(c,x)<ϵ/3 and rational r satisfying
d(c,x)<r<ϵ−d(c,x).
(51)
The triangle inequality gives x∈B(c,r)⊆B(x,ϵ)⊆U. Conversely, from any countable basis select one point of each nonempty member. These points form a countable dense subset, because every nonempty open set contains a basis member. This direction holds for arbitrary topological spaces. Thus a metric space is separable exactly when it is a second-countable space. Intersecting a countable basis with a subspace gives a countable basis for its subspace topology; selecting points as above shows that every subspace of a separable metric space is separable.
For the Sorgenfrey line, Q meets every nonempty interval [a,b), so it is a countable dense subset. In the Sorgenfrey plane, however, for any x∈R and ϵ>0,
([x,x+ϵ)×[−x,−x+ϵ))∩Y={(x,−x)}.
(52)
Indeed, (t,−t) in that rectangle requires both t≥x and t≤x. Every singleton is therefore open in the subspace topology on Y, which is the discrete topology. A dense subset of a discrete space must contain every point. Since Y is in bijection with the uncountable set R, it has no countable dense subset. Hence X is separable and Y is not separable, illustrating why the metric assumption in the inheritance statement matters.

Choose the principal branch of the complex logarithm on H, with −π<argz<π. Then
logz=log∣z∣+iargz,w=−ilogz=argz−ilog∣z∣.
(53)
Thus −π<Rew<π and the imaginary part ranges over all real numbers. Conversely, for w=x+iy in the strip, z=eiw=e−yeix is in H and its principal logarithm is iw. Therefore w=−ilogz:H⟶S​ is an analytic bijection, with analytic inverse z=eiw. Every other continuous branch on the connected domain is logz+2πik for some fixed integer k, so its image is the translated strip S+2πk​.
For G, introduce the Möbius transformation ζ=(z−1)/(z+1), whose inverse is z=(1+ζ)/(1−ζ). Writing ζ=a+ib, its defining circle inequalities transform as follows:
∣z∣<1⟺∣1+ζ∣<∣1−ζ∣⟺a<0,
(54)
and
∣z+i∣>2​⟺∣(1+i)+(1−i)ζ∣2>2∣1−ζ∣2⟺a+b>0.
(55)
Hence G maps bijectively onto the wedge π/2<argζ<3π/4. The principal branch of the complex logarithm is analytic throughout this wedge. Multiplying its logarithm by −8i expands the interval of real parts to (4π,6π), and subtracting 5π centers it at zero. The required conformal map is therefore
W(z)=−8ilog(z+1z−1​)−5π,z∈G.​
(56)
Its real part is 8argζ−5π∈(−π,π), and its imaginary part −8log∣ζ∣ takes every real value. More explicitly, its inverse on S is obtained from ζ=exp(i(W+5π)/8) and z=(1+ζ)/(1−ζ), which verifies both surjectivity and injectivity.

If the primed frame moves at speed v in the positive x direction relative to the unprimed frame, the one-dimensional Lorentz transformation is
x′=γv​(x−vt),t′=γv​(t−vx/c2),γv​=(1−v2/c2)−1/2.​
(61)
For a trajectory with velocity q=dx/dt, differentiating these expressions gives q′=(q−v)/(1−vq/c2). Solving for q, when the particle has primed-frame speed u, proves the relativistic velocity-addition formula
q=1+uv/c2u+v​.​
(62)
For the train problem the sign of the frame velocity reverses: the train frame S moves at +v relative to the station frame S′. Put γ=(1−v2/c2)−1/2. The transformation appropriate to the subsequent parts is therefore
x′=γ(x+vt),t′=γ(t+vx/c2),x=γ(x′−vt′),t=γ(t′−vx′/c2).
(63)

The world lines in the train frame are xA​=L/2, xB​=−L/2 and xC​=−vt. In the station frame, length contraction gives
xA′​=vt′+2γL​,xB′​=vt′−2γL​,xC′​=0.
(64)
The emission event is O=(0,0) in both frames. The signal world lines in S′ are x′=ut′ and x′=−ut′; their intersections with the train endpoints define the reception events RA​,RB​. Their velocities in S, from the relativistic velocity-addition formula, are (u−v)/(1−uv/c2) and −(u+v)/(1+uv/c2).
The two platform-alignment events occur at (x′,t′)=(±L/(2γ),0) in S′. The Lorentz transformation puts them at (x,t)=(±L/2,∓vL/(2c2)) in S, on the tilted simultaneity line t=−vx/c2. The spacetime diagrams show all three observers, both signals, their receptions, and these distinct endpoint-alignment events:

tA​=tB​=2cL​,tB′​−tA′​=−c2γLv​=0.​

The two reception events are simultaneous in S but not in S′: in the station frame the rear moves toward its light signal while the front moves away. Directly, Δx=xB​−xA​=−L and Δt=0, so the Lorentz transformation gives Δt′=γ(Δt+vΔx/c2)=−γLv/c2. This is relativity of simultaneity, concerning spatially separated events; it does not contradict the invariant light speed or the causal ordering of events on a single observer's world line.

For constant density ρ, the inviscid Euler equations with conservative body force are
∂t​u+(u⋅∇)u=−∇(p/ρ+V).
(71)
The vector identity (u⋅∇)u=∇(∣u∣2/2)−u×(∇×u) simplifies for potential flow u=∇ϕ, since its vorticity vanishes. Also ∂t​u=∇ϕt​. Therefore
∇(ϕt​+21​∣u∣2+ρp​+V)=0.
(72)
On each connected fluid region the expression is spatially constant but may depend on time, giving the Unsteady Bernoulli equation
∂t∂ϕ​+21​u2+χ=f(t),χ=p/ρ+V.​
(73)
The arbitrariness of f corresponds to the freedom to add a function of time to the velocity potential without changing u. Replacing ϕ by ϕ−∫tf(s)ds sets the right-hand side to zero.

Use the ideal one-dimensional pipe model: constant density, steady inviscid flow, approximately uniform endpoint speeds u1​,u2​, and equal body-force potential at the two ends. Conservation of mass gives the constant volumetric flow rate q=u1​S1​=u2​S2​, and the mass flow rate is m=ρq. The steady Bernoulli equation gives
Δp=2ρ​(u22​−u12​)=2ρ​q2(S22​1​−S12​1​).
(74)
For flow from a wider to a narrower section, S1​>S2​ and Δp>0. Solving for the positive mass throughput gives the Venturi effect formula
m=S1​S2​S12​−S22​2ρΔp​​.​
(75)
The formula requires these hydraulic assumptions; steady incompressibility alone does not impose uniform endpoint profiles or equal potential. If V1​=V2​, the same derivation replaces Δp by Δp+ρ(V1​−V2​). Viscous losses would also modify the pressure balance. The equal-area case is singular in this pressure-based determination: in the ideal equal-potential model its pressure difference must vanish and does not determine the throughput.

Assume the explanatory variables are not all equal, so Sxx​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2>0. In the Gaussian linear model, the log-likelihood is
ℓ(α,β,σ2)=−2n​log(2πσ2)−2σ21​∑i=1n​(Yi​−α−βxi​)2.
(76)
For fixed σ2, maximum likelihood estimation therefore minimizes the residual sum of squares. Differentiating in α,β gives the least-squares normal equations
∑i​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)=0,∑i​xi​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)=0.
(77)
The first gives α=Yˉ−β​xˉ; substituting it into the second gives β​=Sxy​/Sxx​, with Sxy​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ). Let SSE=∑i​(Yi​−α−β​xi​)2. Differentiating the profiled log-likelihood in σ2 gives
β​=Sxx​Sxy​​,α=Yˉ−β​xˉ,σ2=nSSE​.​
(78)
For the variance estimator this is the interior maximum when SSE>0, which occurs almost surely under the model when n>2.
The coefficient estimators are linear functions of the independent normal errors. In particular,
β​−β=Sxx​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)εi​​,α−α=εˉ−xˉ(β​−β).
(79)
Their multivariate normal distribution has mean (α,β)T and covariance matrix
σ2(1/n+xˉ2/Sxx​−xˉ/Sxx​​−xˉ/Sxx​1/Sxx​​).
(80)
The fitted vector is the orthogonal projection onto the two-dimensional span of (1,…,1)T and (x1​,…,xn​)T. The residual vector is the complementary projection of the spherical normal error vector. Orthogonal normal projections are independent, and in an orthonormal basis of that complementary space its n−2 coordinates are independent N(0,σ2). Consequently
σ2SSE​=σ2nσ2​∼χn−22​,
(81)
independently of (α,β​). This also gives the unbiased estimator s2=SSE/(n−2) rather than the variance MLE.
Under the null hypothesis α=0, for n>2 the Student t test for a simple-regression intercept uses
T=s1/n+xˉ2/Sxx​​α​∼tn−2​,reject if ∣T∣>tn−2,1−η/2​.​
(82)
Here η is the prescribed significance level. The normal numerator divided by its true standard deviation is independent of (n−2)s2/σ2, which proves the stated Student t-distribution. If Sxx​=0, the two coefficients are not separately identifiable; if n≤2, this residual-variance-based test is unavailable.

Set xi​=sin(2θi​). The maximum likelihood estimation formulas for simple linear regression give
β​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)​=Sxx​Sxy​​,α=Yˉ−β​xˉ.​
(83)
Using the supplied rounded summaries gives β​≈21082.7 metres and α≈312.0 metres. Recomputing directly from the printed table gives approximately 21082.4 and 312.0 metres, respectively, so the small summary rounding differences do not affect the conclusion.
I would not accept the model merely because the Student t-test fails to reject a zero regression intercept. That hypothesis test tests one parameter restriction within the assumed model, not the adequacy of its error assumptions or its functional form. In particular, complementary elevations θ and 90∘−θ have exactly the same xi​ and hence the same fitted mean, but their observed low-angle minus high-angle ranges are
864,1871,1913,1173 metres
(84)
for the four corresponding pairs. All four are positive, suggesting an elevation-dependent effect omitted by the mean model, such as air resistance, rather than random scatter determined only by sin(2θ). This is a regression diagnostics concern, not a claim that these finite data logically rule out the normal-error model. The correct conclusion is nonrejection of the intercept restriction does not validate the regression model; further checks of the residual pattern and error assumptions are needed.

Solution

Capital and labour are nonnegative inputs. On the budget line, 0≤K≤b and L=(b−K)/w. Both endpoints give zero output, whereas every interior point has positive output, so the maximum is interior. The Lagrangian with the sign convention of part (i) is
L(K,L,λ)=KαLβ+λ(b−K−wL).
(89)
Its stationarity equations are αKα−1Lβ=λ and βKαLβ−1=wλ. Dividing by the positive output gives α/K=λ/f and β/L=wλ/f, hence wL=(β/α)K. Together with the budget constraint this yields
K∗​=α+βαb​,L∗​=w(α+β)βb​.​
(90)
To verify the unique global maximum, maximize the logarithm of the Cobb–Douglas production function along the budget line:
logf=αlogK+βlog(b−K)−βlogw,dK2d2​logf=−K2α​−(b−K)2β​<0.
(91)
Its unique stationary point is therefore the unique maximum, including comparison with the zero-output boundary points.
Writing r=α+β and C=(α/r)α(β/(wr))β, the optimal output is ϕ(b)=Cbr. The Lagrange multiplier obtained from the first stationarity equation is λ=αϕ/K∗​=rϕ/b. Direct differentiation verifies the envelope theorem identity:
ϕ(b)=(α+βα​)α(w(α+β)β​)βbα+β,ϕ′(b)=λ(b)=b(α+β)ϕ(b)​.​
(92)
For clarity, the global dual-supremum premise of part (i) need not hold for every exponent pair allowed here. If r>1, along (K,L)=(tK∗​,tL∗​) the unrestricted Lagrangian is trϕ(b)+λb(1−t), which tends to infinity for every finite λ. Thus the verification above is by constrained stationarity and direct differentiation, and remains valid even when that stronger global Lagrangian duality representation fails.
